new_statements.quote: Our knowledge of Oriomo prosody is vanishingly small: there is word-initial stress in Bine (Döhler, in press: 6), but for Wipi and Gizrra prosody is entirely undescribed. More detailed description may yet reveal complex prosody in these languages as well. [p. 47] ... In Western Bine, at least, vowel length is marginally phonemic: a subset of vowels (a, i, u) contrast long and short pairs in word-initial (i.e., stressed) open syllables, e.g. kame '1SG.POSS' vs. kaame 'bush wallaby' (Döhler, in press: 6). [p. 25]
new_statements.citation: Josefsson, Michael W. 2025. Deep-time diversity: The Oriomo languages of Southern New Guinea. BA (Honours) thesis, Australian National University (Glottolog ref 713327 lists it as an MA thesis). Open access: https://openresearch-repository.anu.edu.au/handle/1885/733794320
new_statements.locator: p. 47, §4.4.3 (PDF page 57); supporting passage p. 25, §4.2.2 (PDF page 35)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress falls on the first syllable of the word (reported second-hand from Döhler's in-press sketch, p. 6). Corroborated by the phonetic transcription of the text in Fleischmann & Turpeinen 1977: 138-140 (saved excerpt), where every word carries the primary-stress mark on its initial syllable, and by their statement (p. 102) that vowel length is contrastive 'in the initial syllable of words and also in the initial syllable of each stem in compound words'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated in any opened source. In the 1977 text transcription (pp. 138-140) a secondary mark (") appears on a later syllable of words of four or more syllables (e.g. 'ya:n:a"dzuge, 'mat(h)i"k(h)aeli, 'p(h)e:s:e"nene, 't(h)at(h)ja"rige), which looks like penultimate secondary stress, but this is my reading of the transcription, not a statement.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Wurm 1971: 146 (first-hand, family survey, saved) says Bine has 'a complex stress system with rhythm principles, and apparently a two-tone system of very low functional load' without giving a position; Josefsson 2025 does not treat Bine as tonal (only Meryam in the family). Bine function words are often shortened in rapid speech (Josefsson 2025: 51 fn. 1, after Döhler).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (word-initial stress; the vowel-length contrast is anchored to the word-initial stressed syllable and to the initial syllable of each stem in compounds per Fleischmann & Turpeinen 1977: 102). Citation forms and phrasal prominence not discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Josefsson 2025 and Döhler (in press) describe Western Bine (the Kunini/Masingle/Drageli varieties; Döhler groups eight Bine varieties into Western and Eastern); Fleischmann & Turpeinen 1977 describe Eastern Bine (SIL work 1970s). Both are dialects of bine1240 (no separate glottocodes in Glottolog 5.1). Wurm 1971 refers to Bine generally (Kunini dialect data).

sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: open copy online
sources.note: Only 7 excerpt pages online; no stress statement in them. p. 102: 'Length is contrastive for all vowels in the initial syllable of words and also in the initial syllable of each stem in compound words.' The text transcription pp. 138-140 marks primary stress on the first syllable of every word and a secondary mark on a later syllable of long words. The full 46-page paper (which presumably has a stress section) could not be obtained: SIL record id 15669 does not resolve; pnglanguages.sil.org search pages are behind a JS challenge.
